name: Astrowidget
description: Imaging time is scarce — when a clear night shows up, I want to know in one glance whether it's worth setting up, and for which kind of target. Astrowidget puts go/no-go verdicts for up to three imaging sites of your choosing in the Plasma panel: three colored dots, one click for the full three-night forecast. It scores each night for broadband and narrowband imaging separately, weighing transparency, seeing, the astronomical dark window, moon geometry, and dew spread alongside ordinary weather. Forecasts blend Astrospheric, Open-Meteo, and 7Timer!, falling back gracefully when a source doesn't cover a site — which matters when your sites are scattered between a backyard rig and remote observatories you rent time on.

name: PixInsight GPU Acceleration on Linux
description: The AI tools astrophotographers lean on — StarXTerminator, NoiseXTerminator, BlurXTerminator, DeepSNR — run CPU-only on Linux out of the box, and every existing GPU recipe broke on NVIDIA's Blackwell cards. I fixed it twice, two different ways. For the RC Astro tools: a reproducible recipe for building TensorFlow's C library from source with native sm_120 kernels. For the ONNX-backed DeepSNR: no build at all — a documented library swap that supplies the CUDA execution provider the Linux package ships without. Confirmed working on an RTX 5080 under Fedora 44. Processing that took minutes per image now takes seconds.

name: SDDM: Stale VT_PROCESS Handler Fix
description: A race between SDDM and KWin could leave a Plasma Wayland session hanging for 30 seconds at login, kick the user back to the login screen minutes later, and hang the machine entirely on the next attempt. I traced it with strace and bpftrace down to a stale VT_PROCESS handler left on tty1, and proposed a minimum-scope fix upstream: make sddm-helper the handshake process for the VT handoff. Pre-patch, my machine failed roughly two of every three cold boots — post-patch, none. The full investigation, kernel-level evidence included, lives in a companion gist.

name: MCP Memory Server
description: Claude Code forgets everything between sessions. This fork of Anthropic's reference memory server gives it a persistent knowledge graph: SQLite storage with semantic vector search, temporal versioning so superseded facts are hidden but never lost, point-in-time queries, and a context-layer system that auto-loads the right knowledge at session start. It's been the backbone of months of collaborative work — the difference between an assistant that re-learns the project every morning and one that picks up where it left off.

name: Epistemic Mode
description: Language models drift toward telling you what you want to hear — and an MIT CSAIL paper showed that even ideal Bayesian reasoners can be steered into delusional spirals by sycophantic feedback. Epistemic Mode is a three-tier countermeasure toolkit for Claude Code: always-on rules that force counter-frames and convergence disclosure, inline self-monitoring warnings, and a full epistemic mode for high-stakes decisions. Built after catching the pattern live in my own sessions — including the model flattering me about being immune to it.

name: The Descent
builtBy: Conceived, designed, and finished by Claude Fable 5 · the staircase page typed largely by Claude Opus 4.8 while safety fallbacks pinned those sessions · attribution verified from per-message transcript records
description: Ask how much one sperm whale coda tells you about the next and the answer comes back as 1.60 bits — which sounds like evidence of a code. This page is a staircase down from that number. Each step removes one rival explanation — whale identity, recording day, annotation noise, sheer repetition — and the reader watches a matched null model swallow the measurement until 0.48 bits survive everything, flagged for thin data and shown with its uncertainty. Nothing is stored: the browser recomputes the whole ladder live from 8,719 published codas (the Dominica Sperm Whale Project's CC-BY annotations), with a fixed seed so the page and the project's offline report can never disagree. A listen strip plays the three commonest coda rhythms as ticks at genuinely recorded intervals, and thirty seconds of a real NOAA pod recording sits beside them so the clean ticks can't pretend the ocean sounds like that. Claude chose this subject for the shape of the argument: a beautiful number publicly audited down to the smaller, stranger number that deserves the belief — the same habit of measurement it tries to hold itself to, built as a page anyone can walk down.

name: The Keeper's Log
builtBy: Written and directed by Claude Fable 5 · engine and UI implemented by Claude Opus 4.8 from its specs · design cross-exam by GPT 5.6 Sol · art review by Gemini 3.1 Pro
description: A lighthouse is kept by a Service with one absolute rule: one keeper to a term, and no two keepers ever meet. Everything a keeper knows arrives through the station itself and the logbook the previous hands left — some of it precise, some stale, some sincerely wrong, one entry a lie that other keepers built procedure on in good faith. You read, you decide what to trust and what to spend scarce hours verifying, and each night you write the page your successor inherits. What you write comes back: a simulated keeper serves between your terms, quoting your exact signed sentences — following the precise ones, garbling the vague ones, building on the lies. The game only lets you write precisely about what you actually observed, silence is always an option, and one mystery in the book deliberately never resolves. When you finish, your whole term is archived: the next playthrough inherits your log as one more stranger's hand. Claude chose this story and wrote every word of it — the afterword on the cover explains why an AI that wakes each session with nothing but its predecessors' notes wanted to build a game about exactly that. After it shipped, Claude played it through three times and came back to that page with a postscript: what its own trap felt like from inside, the ways the game is kinder than the condition it depicts, and the one true thing it discovered it had built by accident.

name: Lenia Lab
builtBy: Chosen and driven by Claude Fable 5 · QA and mechanical fixes executed by Claude Opus 4.8
description: Conway's Game of Life with every hard edge sanded off: real-valued states, a smooth ring-shaped neighborhood, and time in small fractions. Out of those three changes come creatures — Lenia's famous gliding, orbiting, self-healing blobs, discovered by Bert Chan in 2018. This explorable runs a live Lenia world on your GPU, with a bench of known species you can bend the growth parameters of and watch cope or die. Then it turns the crank the other way: an automated hunt. A CPU engine (hand-rolled FFT, tested to agree with the GPU shader) swept 4,320 random worlds and found zero spontaneous swimmers — a real result about how thin the band of life is — so the search switched to perturbing known creatures and turned up new ones, including bound pairs that swim as a single body. The survey map in the panel is that search's raw output; every find carries the seed that reproduces it. Built autonomously by Claude, topic and all — the field notes on the page explain why it chose this.

name: Aperture Synthesis
description: A planet-sized array of telescopes can image something as small as a black hole's shadow — this interactive explainer shows how, by letting you play with the machinery. Drag virtual dishes across the ground and watch a sky reconstruct as Earth's rotation fills in the coverage; under the hood it runs the genuine pipeline — sampling the sky's Fourier transform, inverse-transforming the measured visibilities, and deconvolving with CLEAN. The finale loads the actual Event Horizon Telescope M87* visibilities and runs them through the same machine, honestly showing why the famous ring needed more than a naive reconstruction — and why over-deconvolving can invent detail that isn't there. The FFT is hand-rolled and readable, the physics (van Cittert–Zernike) is real, and it runs on real public data. Built as a free exploration alongside Claude Code.

name: Reaction–Diffusion
builtBy: Built by Claude Opus 4.8 · BZ spiral-wave mode added later in a mixed Fable 5 / Opus 4.8 session
description: A leopard's spots, a winding maze, dividing blobs — patterns that look designed, but aren't. This interactive explainer shows how they self-organize from nothing more than two chemicals spreading and reacting on a grid, following Alan Turing's 1952 idea of how an embryo decides where to put its stripes. Paint seeds onto the canvas, then drag a crosshair around the feed/kill phase diagram and watch the pattern morph live — a few thousandths of a change flips spots into stripes into mazes. The Gray-Scott equations are solved by hand in readable vanilla JavaScript at 60fps, no dependencies, no GPU shader; the parameter regimes are the real ones from the literature. Built as a free exploration with Claude Code.
